articleHtml:
By Marcus Thorne, Consumer Credit & Auto Lending Specialist · Last updated: November 27, 2026

The sticker price is not the amount you borrow

Dealers often steer the conversation toward "what monthly payment works for you". That question hides the numbers that decide whether the deal is good: the amount financed, the APR and the length of the loan. This calculator exposes all three. The sections below show what happens to a real example when each one changes.

Worked example: a $35,000 car with a trade-in

You buy a $35,000 vehicle. Your trade-in is worth $8,000, you put $3,000 down and local sales tax is 7%. In many states tax applies to the price after the trade-in credit, so:

LineAmount
Vehicle price$35,000
Trade-in credit−$8,000
Taxable amount$27,000
Sales tax at 7%+$1,890
Cash down payment−$3,000
Amount financed$25,890

Rules differ by state. A few states tax the full price with no trade-in credit, and fees such as registration and title are separate. Always confirm the tax method with the dealer or your state's motor vehicle agency.

How the loan term changes the real cost

Using the $25,890 loan at a 7.5% APR:

TermMonthly paymentTotal interestTotal paid
48 months$625.99$4,158$30,048
60 months$518.78$5,237$31,127
72 months$447.64$6,340$32,230
84 months$397.11$7,467$33,357

Stretching from 48 to 84 months lowers the payment by $229 but adds about $3,300 of interest. There is a second cost that does not appear in the table: cars lose value fastest in the first years. On an 84-month loan you can owe more than the car is worth for a long time, which matters if it is totaled, or if you want to sell or trade early.

What a few points of APR are worth

On the same 60-month, $25,890 loan:

  • 5% APR: $488.58 per month, $3,425 total interest
  • 7.5% APR: $518.78 per month, $5,237 total interest
  • 10% APR: $550.09 per month, $7,115 total interest

The gap between 5% and 10% is about $3,700 in interest. This is why it pays to get a pre-approval from your bank or credit union before visiting the dealership. You then know what rate you can beat, and you can compare it with the dealer's offer on equal terms. Note that credit score, loan term, and vehicle age all influence the rate you are offered.

Negative equity: the trap of rolling over old debt

Suppose you still owe $12,000 on a car that is worth $8,000. That $4,000 gap is negative equity. If you trade it in, the dealer can add it to the new loan. In our example the financed amount rises from $25,890 to $29,890. On a 72-month loan at 7.5%, the payment goes from $447.64 to $516.80 and you are paying interest on a car you no longer own. When possible, wait until you owe less than the car is worth, or pay the gap in cash.

Fees and add-ons that quietly raise the payment

  • Documentation fees. Rolling a $600 fee into the loan adds about $12 per month on 60 months at 7.5%, plus the interest.
  • Extended warranties and GAP insurance. These may be worthwhile in some cases, but they are optional products with their own prices and can usually be negotiated or bought elsewhere.
  • Insurance. A financed car requires full coverage, which costs more than basic liability. Include it when judging affordability.

A simple affordability check

A widely used guideline is "20/4/10": at least 20% down, a loan of no more than 4 years, and total vehicle costs (payment, insurance and fuel) under about 10% of gross income. It is a guideline, not a rule, but a deal that fails all three deserves a second look.

Common mistakes

  • Negotiating the monthly payment instead of the out-the-door price.
  • Ignoring the trade-in's real value; get quotes from other buyers before you accept the dealer's.
  • Choosing the longest term to "afford" a more expensive car.
  • Not checking for prepayment penalties before planning to pay off early.

Frequently asked questions

How is a monthly car payment calculated?

It uses the standard loan formula: payment = P × r(1+r)^n ÷ [(1+r)^n − 1], with P as the amount financed, r as the monthly rate (APR ÷ 12) and n as the number of months.

Does the trade-in reduce sales tax?

In many states yes, because tax is charged on the price minus the trade-in value. In others the full price is taxed. Check your state's rule.

Is it better to take a longer loan with a lower payment?

A longer term lowers the monthly payment but increases total interest and the time you may owe more than the car is worth. Choose the shortest term you can comfortably afford.

What is a good APR for a car loan?

It depends on your credit score, the loan term and whether the car is new or used. Compare offers from at least two lenders, including a credit union.

Methodology and sources

Payments use the standard amortization formula and match published loan tables. APRs shown are examples, not current quotes. For guidance on shopping for auto financing, see the CFPB auto loan resources. Educational estimate only. Corrections: support@smartcalclab.com.
